question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 7. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so the PLL information is in the U-layer side stickers. A two-face view gives six stickers, but that leaves a rotational/mirror ambiguity for several paired PLL cases unless you also already know the exact alignment. One additional sticker from a third side resolves the ambiguity and pins down the exact case, so the minimum is 7 non-top-facing stickers.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so the PLL information is in the top-layer side stickers. Two full adjacent side faces give 6 stickers and identify the basic corner/edge pattern, but some G- and N-perm cases still leave the two boundary corner pieces underdetermined. You need one extra sticker from each of those hidden corners to resolve the exact PLL, so 6 + 2 = 8 non-top-facing stickers.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 7. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so PLL recognition must come from the side stickers of the last layer. You need to determine both the edge permutation and the corner permutation. In general, the four top-layer edge stickers are needed to fix the edge permutation, and for the corners, once three corner side stickers are known, the fourth corner placement is forced by permutation parity since corner orientation is already solved by OLL. That gives 4 edge stickers + 3 corner stickers = 7 non-top-facing stickers as the minimum. Six stickers from two adjacent sides can often narrow it down, but it still leaves some mirror/permutation-pair ambiguities in cases like the G-perms unless the seventh sticker is seen.

1.text:
In CFOP the U-face is mono-colour after OLL so that the U-face itself
carries no permutation information.  What is left to be read is the
side colour of the eight U-pieces.

* a U-edge is a U + 1 side sticker.  There are 4 U-edges and they are
read by the 4 side stickers of the U-edges;
* a U-corner is a U + 2 side stickers.  There are 4 U-corners and they
are read by the 8 side stickers of the U-corners.

Hence the permutation information of the last layer lives on the
12 side stickers of the U-layer,

4 edge ×1  +  4 corner ×2 = 12 non-U stickers,

i.e. one identifying sticker per U-piece, 8 piece identifiers in all,
4 for the edges and 4 for the corners.  By the usual corner-edge
parity the eighth identifier is a consequence of the other seven so
that information-theoretically seven independent non-U stickers are
enough, the familiar eight-sticker, twelve-sticker-by-count view of
the U-layer.  This is what is normally quoted as “ the four U-edges
and the four U-corners ” – 12 side stickers in total, 8 distinct
piece identifiers, 7 independent. ∎

2.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face monochrome. The only information
that is left in the last layer is the permutation of the four U edges and
the four U corners.  Up to rotation

* an U edge is the edge sticker $U\!-\!X$ that it shows on the side face
  $X\in\{F,B,L,R\}$ – one non $U$ sticker per edge, 4 stickers;
* a U corner is the pair $U\!-\!X$ $U\!-\!Y$ that it shows on the two
  side faces $X,Y$ – two non $U$ stickers per corner, $4\times2=8$
  stickers.

Hence the U–layer itself contains

$4\;{\rm edges}\times1+4\;{\rm corners}\times2=12$

stickers which are not on the $U$ face, the $3\times4=12$ stickers which
form the top rows of the F, B, L and R faces.  It is the pattern of
these 12 side stickers which is the PLL.  In terms of pieces you only
need one identifying side sticker per last–layer cubie, i.e. four edge
stickers and four corner stickers, the eight last–layer cubies.  Up to
the obvious parity of a permutation seven of the eight cubies are
informationally independent, the eighth being forced by the parity of
the $4!$ corners and the $4!$ edges.  This is the usual “ eight piece,
seven independent’’ description of PLL recognition.  The twelve
physical side stickers are the twelve which have to be inspected if you
want the whole top row of the four side faces.

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is finished by the OLL so that after the OLL

* U is monochromatic and
* the only thing that is left to do in the PLL is to permute the eight
pieces that are now in the U slab.

The eight pieces that are in the U slab are

* four U edges.  Every U edge carries one sticker that is not on U,
the normal colour of the face on which the edge is sitting.  Hence
the U edges contribute

```
4 × 1 = 4
```

non-U stickers to the slab.

* four U corners.  Every U corner carries two stickers that are not on
U, the two side colours of the corner.  Hence the U corners contribute

```
4 × 2 = 8
```

non-U stickers to the slab.

So the U slab itself carries

```
4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12
```

distinct non-U stickers, four on each side face in the top row.  In
particular the four edge side stickers are enough to read the edge
permutation and the eight corner side stickers are enough to read the
corner permutation.  Up to a U–rotation and the usual even/odd parity
of the last layer the eighth piece is determined by the other seven,
so it is in the information theoretic sense enough to read seven of
the twelve peripheral stickers, in practice quoted as the four edge
side stickers and one side sticker of each of the four corners, i.e.
the eight stickers that you normally look at for PLL recognition.  This
is the twelve sticker U slab, the seven/eight sticker set that is
normally referred to as "the side of the U layer".

5.text:
In CFOP the U–face is solved after OLL

* $U$ is monochrome,
* the only information that is left in the last layer is the
permutation of the four U–edges and of the four U–corners.

The U–slice is

* 4 U–edges, each edge carries one non–$U$ sticker, 4 stickers, and
* 4 U–corners, each corner carries two non–$U$ stickers, $4\times 2=8$
  stickers,

i.e.  $4+8=12$ non–$U$ stickers in all on the U–slice.  Up to the
global orientation of the cube one sticker per U–piece is enough to
know which physical piece is sitting in which U–position.  There are
$4$ U–edges and $4$ U–corners, i.e. eight pieces of information, the
usual way of stating it is that the eight side colours of the U–slice,
four edge and four corner, have to be read.  Of course the two
side colours of a U–corner are physically two distinct stickers, so
the U–slice carries $12$ non–up stickers in total, and it is those
$12$ side stickers that are normally inspected in PLL recognition.

In information terms the parity of a permutation forces the eighth
piece once seven of them are known, so seven non–$U$ side stickers are
already information-theoretically sufficient to pin down the $21$
PLL classes, the conventional practical statement being the $8$ U–piece
side stickers, i.e. the $12$ physical non–up stickers of the U–slice.
This is the $8$-piece, $12$-sticker, statement that is normally quoted
as “read the four U–edges and the four U–corners’’ in PLL recognition.

Physical inventory of the U-slice
* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker per edge = 4
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers per corner = 8
4 + 8 = 12 distinct non-U physical stickers, the top rows of F B L R. That is the 12-sticker U-slab that carries all PLL information.
